title: From understanding intentions to verified fulfillment
scope: Selected 2025–2026 primary papers, checked through 17 October 2026. A targeted review, not an exhaustive search or a cross-benchmark ranking.

papers.title: Structured Uncertainty guided Clarification for LLM Agents
papers.label: SAGE · 2025 / revised Apr 2026
papers.mechanism: Represent uncertainty over tool arguments, then choose questions by expected value of perfect information minus repeated-question cost. Separate missing user specification from model uncertainty.
papers.result: On ambiguous ClarifyBench cases, GPT-4o coverage rises from 55.70% with Domain-aware ReAct to 59.73%; questions fall from 2.56 to 1.39. Coverage measures correct-parameter tool calls, not complete task success.
papers.limitation: On the separate BFCLv2/When2Call evaluation (Table 4), GPT-4o ToolCall F1 falls from 0.75 with ReAct to 0.65 with SAGE. Simulated users and tool schemas limit transfer; selecting one call does not track concurrent obligations.
papers.transfer: Attach uncertainty to each current requirement. Do not turn alternative interpretations into several mandatory tasks.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Clarification in LLM Agents with Information Gain
papers.label: IG Clarifier · Jun 2026
papers.mechanism: Train a small clarifier with DAPO using the change in length-normalized likelihood of the true goal after a question and answer. Tool feedback can trigger clarification.
papers.result: For the Qwen3-8B agent with a trained Qwen3-1.7B clarifier, retail/airline macro-average task success rises from 15.4% to 17.8%, while steps rise from 24.2 to 25.1. The untrained 1.7B clarifier scores 14.9%.
papers.limitation: Training uses known goals and simulated users. The reported five-agent aggregate in Table 3 does not reconcile with its rows, so it is not used here. A case resolves budget ambiguity but still executes an upgrade before confirmation.
papers.transfer: Reward useful uncertainty reduction, while measuring execution order separately. Asking successfully does not establish fulfillment.

papers.title: RECAP: REwriting Conversations for Intent Understanding in Agentic Planning
papers.label: RECAP · Findings EACL 2026
papers.version: Quantitative analysis uses arXiv v1; venue independently verified
papers.location: Main DPO experiment; Appendix F, Table 9
papers.mechanism: Rewrite conversation history into a current goal description before planning. Train the rewriter with DPO preferences derived from downstream plans instead of requiring one gold summary.
papers.result: DPO-human versus Advanced rewriting wins/ties/loses 48.88/28.90/22.22% on the small test set, but 26.80/44.53/28.67% across all 750 conversations: no broad superiority in that comparison.
papers.limitation: Synthetic conversations and plan-preference judgments; plans are not executed. More elaborate rewriting can invent assumptions. The test set comes from a 150-conversation subset.
papers.transfer: Evaluate summaries by their downstream effects, and penalize unsupported requirements. Better-looking summaries alone are insufficient.

papers.title: Can Agent Memory Systems Track Evolving State?
papers.label: StateMem · Aug 2026 preprint
papers.location: State representation; Table 14 and dependency ablation
papers.mechanism: Maintain sourced state units with active, superseded and needs_recheck status. Record dependencies so a changed input can invalidate derived conclusions.
papers.result: With DeepSeek-V4-Flash, StateMem answers 117/322 probes correctly, versus Dense retrieval 66/322 and full context 48/322. Removing dependency propagation scores 120/322, slightly above the complete method.
papers.limitation: 234 synthetic scenarios, one run, a same-family judge, and 165–600 encoding calls per scenario. The benchmark targets the method's policy family; authors call its gains an upper bound. Propagation can wrongly flag valid state for rechecking.
papers.transfer: Track which requirement changed and preserve unaffected requirements; test stale-state retention and over-deletion separately.

papers.title: MEM1: Learning to Synergize Memory and Reasoning for Efficient Long-Horizon Agents
papers.label: MEM1 · 2025 / ICLR 2026
papers.mechanism: Use reinforcement learning to update a compact internal state that combines memory and reasoning, then discard the old trajectory. Final task rewards teach the model what to retain.
papers.result: On 16-objective QA, MEM1-7B averages 1.97 exact-match subanswers versus 0.567 for Qwen2.5-14B, with peak tokens 1,040 versus 3,840. These are counts of correct subanswers, not whole-task success rates.
papers.limitation: It needs verifiable training rewards and does not establish a minimal sufficient state. Adding a format reward lowers two-objective EM from 0.709 to 0.466.
papers.transfer: A learned compact state is a real alternative to a queue or retained reasoning; compare under matched total inference cost.

papers.title: LLMs Get Lost in Evolving User Intent
papers.label: Evolving intent · Jul 2026 preprint
papers.location: GSM8K intent evolution; BIRD oracle recap; preliminary GRPO experiment
papers.mechanism: Separate revealing parameters, revising parameters and switching task functions. Construct evolving conversations that return to the original benchmark target and retain its verifier.
papers.result: Across 200 GSM8K items, GPT-5.5 accuracy falls from 99.0% in one turn to 80.5% with six intent changes. On 100 BIRD items, function-switch accuracy rises from 65% to 75% with oracle recap, still below 80% single-turn accuracy.
papers.limitation: Preliminary Qwen3-4B GRPO improves dynamic-intent math accuracy from 64% to 76%; this is not broad agent evidence. Final-answer verification does not check every intermediate action.
papers.transfer: Separate additions, corrections and task switches in evaluation. Use oracle recap as an intervention, not deployable ground truth.

papers.title: AgentPRM: Process Reward Models for LLM Agents via Step-Wise Promise and Progress
papers.label: AgentPRM · Nov 2025 preprint
papers.version: arXiv v1; the Xi et al. paper, distinct from the other AgentPRM title
papers.mechanism: Train a reward model to estimate future success and improvement between adjacent decisions. TD estimation with GAE supplies labels; the reward model guides beam search and can support RL.
papers.result: For Qwen2.5-3B on WebShop at the same 4×4 beam setting, success is 72.5% with AgentPRM versus 59.0% with PVM. Evaluation uses 100 WebShop queries.
papers.limitation: Controlled WebShop, BabyAI and TextCraft environments differ from evolving conversation. Training and search incur extra cost. Promise/progress scores are predictions, not direct evidence that an obligation was fulfilled.
papers.transfer: Learn which action improves remaining-goal fulfillment; do not reward tool-call count or verbal claims of progress.

papers.title: InsightToast: Proactive Information Retrieval & Glanceable Visualization in the Side Channel of Data-Rich Meetings
papers.label: InsightToast · Aug 2026 preprint
papers.mechanism: Maintain conversational state, detect a knowledge gap, generate complementary queries, evaluate retrieval, and deliver sourced text or charts in a peripheral interface.
papers.result: In 16 sessions, mean utterance-level trigger precision/recall/F1 are .70/.99/.81 against researcher annotations. Sessions average 113 utterances; exact TP/FP/FN counts are not reported.
papers.limitation: These are trigger metrics, not answer quality. Each 15-minute policy discussion pairs a participant with a researcher using scripted cues. Adjacent-turn over-triggering, noisy notifications and 29-second synthesis latency remain limitations.
papers.transfer: The closest application reference for this meeting assistant: separate knowledge-gap detection, retrieved evidence and notification. It does not establish compound-task completion or local ASR robustness.

papers.title: DeployBench
papers.label: DeployBench · Jun 2026 / revised Aug 2026
papers.mechanism: Evaluate research-artifact deployments using hidden checks that execute a reduced paper-specific experiment and inspect its outputs. Diagnose the gap between an agent's stopping criterion and the requested outcome.
papers.result: Five models on 51 artifacts achieve 7.8–51.0% success. Of 181 failures, 102 self-stop; 60 of those claim SUCCESS and 32 report PARTIAL. Self-stop is therefore not synonymous with a false-success claim.
papers.limitation: Public reproducible artifacts and one OpenHands scaffold; deployment is not conversation. The paper proposes stronger completion checks but does not demonstrate a mitigation experiment.
papers.transfer: Derive completion evidence from the original requirement and inspect the delivered state, rather than accepting a weaker substitute test.

interpretation: The promising unit of optimization is a current, evidence-linked requirement together with its uncertainty, revision history and observed fulfillment. This is our synthesis, not a validated architecture or a claim of novelty.

arms: Oracle current state as a diagnostic reference
proposed_comparison.controls: Freeze the model, tools, visible prefix, deadline, final evaluator and total resource budget. Count state-updater, clarifier, verifier and failed-call costs. Use matched-context and token controls to test effects of added context.
outcomes: All applicable requirements fulfilled in user-visible output
Initially omitted versus subsequently lost requirements at matched visible-prefix checkpoints
Dependency-order and required-confirmation violations, including later-repaired cases
proposed_comparison.attribution: Only after a state intervention is characterized, cross a fixed/learned state policy with a fixed/adapted actor. Report both main effects and the interaction. These identify effects of specific interventions, not universal responsibility of the LLM or harness.

limitations: No new model experiment, SFT, RL or reproduction was performed.
Selected sources use different tasks, model sizes, budgets and metrics; their scores cannot be ranked in a shared leaderboard.
Synthetic and simulated-user findings do not establish benefits for live meetings, real ASR or human users.
The proposed state representation must be tested against a simple summary, its own costs, and errors from invented or stale obligations.
